full_judgment:
7. The plaintiff being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and decree of reversal passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 10th Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 211 of 1993 as petitioner moved this Court its revisional jurisdiction as per provision of Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, hence this rule. 

 8. Mr Nikhil Kumar Saha, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner has submitted that the impugned judgment is not a proper judgment of reversal as provided under Provision of Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure as the learned Appellate Judge being the last Court of fact did not properly controvert the categorical finding arrived at by the learned trial Judge while decreeing the suit and the learned Appellate Judge did not properly discuss and evaluate the evidences on record in its entirety and correct perspective thus the learned appellate Judge failed in his duty and arrived at wrong finding and decision leading to error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. As such the same is not sustainable in law. 

 14. I have given my anxious consideration to the submission made at the Bar. I have gone through the rule petition, the impugned judgment, the judgment of the trial Court as well as the evidence-on-record both oral and documentary. After going through the impugned judgment I find substance in the submission of Mr Saha to the effect that the learned Appellate Judge failed to deliver the judgment in adherence to the provision of Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. I find that the learned Appellate Judge passed a very short cut judgment without properly adverting the points and issues that has been decided by the learned trial Judge who on discussion and evaluation of evidences on record arrived at his decision to decree the suit but the learned Appellate Judge miserably failed to make thread bare discussion of the evidences on record and after going through the judgment I find that the learned Appellate Judge only partially discuss the evidences of PW 1 and 2 and he did not evaluate the entire evidence-on-record and I find that the judgment suffers from misreading and non-reading of evidences on record. The learned Appellate Judge being the last Court of fact ought to have advert the categorical finding and decision given by the learned trial Judge in the impugned judgment but here the learned Appellate Judge failed in complying with the provision of Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure as such the impugned judgment passed by the learned Appellate Judge is not a proper judgment of reversal as has been decided by our lordships in the Appellate Division in so many decision. Specially the learned Appellate Judge arrived at wrong finding setting aside the judgment of the trial Court that the defendant No. 4 did not take any tactic for getting the sale, deed registered in his name in connivance with the defendant Nos. 1-3 which is not at all the correct finding as I find after going through the evidences on record and pleadings of the parties. I find that this is not correct finding of the learned Appellate Judge rather it is contrary to the evidences on record. On this count the learned Appellate Judge did not properly evaluate the deposition of the two PW's who very stated that the defendant No. 4 who was supposed to collect his portion of the balance consideration money and to inform the plaintiff that he has managed his portion. The defendant No. 4 asked the plaintiff (PW 1) and his corroborated witness PW No. 2 not to do very hurry, he will arrange his balance consideration money soon and then kabala will be registered. The plaintiff as PW 1 and PW 2 stated that they approached the agents /karjakarak of the defendant Nos. 1-3 to get the deed executed in favour of the plaintiff as he has arranged his balance consideration money but the agent/caracara of the defendant Nos. 1-3 asked them to contact the defendant No. 4. In this way the defendant No. 4 and defendant No. 1 and agent/karjakarak of the defendant Nos. 1-3 taking recourse to deceitful tactics to defraud the plaintiff and got the sale deed registered in favour of the defendant No. 4 within one month 7 days time of the expiry of the stipulated period of the deed of agreement. Although the defendant No. 4 tried to establish a case that the plaintiff failed to collect his part of the balance consideration money and therefore he return the original deed of agreement (Bonaparte) and other papers to the defendant Nos. 4 who in his turn return the same to the defendant Nos. 1-3 as they express their unwillingness to executed and registered saf kabala in favour of the plaintiff and defendant No. 4. In view of the fact that the stipulated period for execution and registration of their sale deed has been over and the defendant No. 4 afterwards on separate deal agreed to purchase the case property at a higher price on fresh negotiation with the defendant Nos. 1-3 and accordingly he got the Saf kabala registered in his name alone within the knowledge of the plaintiff. But on scrutiny of the evidence on record I find that there is no such corroborative evidence to support the case of the defendant No. 4. In this respect the evidences of PW 1 and 2 are corroborative and believable but the learned Appellate Judge referring to few lines of deposition of PW 1 and 2 has made his comment that the PW 1 i.e. the plaintiff did not enter into any agreement with the defendant No. 4 and, as such, he was not entitled to get kabala from the defendant No. 4 and referring to the deposition of the plaintiff as PW No.1 and his corroborative witness the PW No. 2 the learned Appellate Judge reversed and set aside the well reasoned and well evaluated judgment of the learned Trial Judge without properly discussing and evaluating the deposition of these two PW's. Thus I find that the learned Appellate Judge did not properly evaluate the evidences on record and the same suffers from the misreading and non-reading of evidences on record. As such the impugned judgment is not sustainable as I find after perusing the evidences on record. Wherein it is admitted position that the plaintiff and the defendant No. 4 have entered into an agreement with the defendant Nos. 1-3 for purchase of the suit property jointly and it is written in the said deed of agreement (Bainapatra) that the purchasers have paid Taka 57,000 as earnest money out of Taka 66,000 fixed as total consideration money for the suit land and the defendant No. 4 was the scribe of the said deed of agreement which is admitted by the defendant No. 4 himself although he tried to establish that the plaintiff could not pay the earnest money of his portion due to shortage of fund but he could not adduce any corroborative evidence to that effect as such the writing of the deed of agreement stands as valid terms and conditions and it is clear from the deed to agreement that both the intending purchaser paid Taka 28,500 each as earnest money to the seller and on receipt on the same amount the executants of the said Bonaparte signed and executed the deed of agreement (Bainapatra).
